profile.summary: Graphormer is a transformer architecture for graphs, published by Microsoft Research for molecule modelling. It takes a graph, such as a molecule, and encodes the graph's structural information into a standard Transformer. The released package is a training toolkit for graph-level prediction tasks rather than one fixed model; it appears on this benchmark database because the DeepProtein benchmark trained a Graphormer layer as a baseline on protein tasks.

summary_quotes.text: Graphormer is a deep learning package that allows researchers and developers to train custom models for molecule modeling tasks.
we solve this mystery by presenting Graphormer, which is built upon the standard Transformer architecture
It utilized transformer on graphs with spatial, centrality, and edge encoding.
Our key insight to utilizing Transformer in the graph is the necessity of effectively encoding the structural information of a graph into the model.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Graphormer keeps the standard transformer blocks and adds encodings that put the graph structure into the model: the paper describes structural encoding methods, which the benchmark paper summarises as spatial, centrality and edge encoding. The authors also give a mathematical characterisation of the expressive power of the architecture and argue that with these encodings many popular graph neural network variants are special cases of Graphormer. The package builds on a pinned fairseq revision, so training and inference run through the fairseq command line.

sections.title: Use as a benchmark baseline
sections.body: The DeepProtein benchmark trained Graphormer as one of its graph baselines. It does not use the Microsoft package: its encoder imports GraphormerLayer from DGL, wraps it with a linear projection and max pooling, and the benchmark states that for simplicity and scalability on large graphs it deployed only one Graphormer layer with ReLU activation, node embedding dimension 64 and LayerNorm after the MLP layers. A protein result against the name Graphormer is therefore a single DGL Graphormer layer the benchmark trained, not a Microsoft Graphormer checkpoint.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository is at version 2.0, released in December 2021, and its README states that pretrained models on PCQM4M and PCQM4Mv2 are available and that advanced pretrained versions are available only on Azure Quantum Elements. The README gives no download address for the pretrained models, so a result should name the code commit, the task script and the checkpoint path used. This page read the repository at commit c55f56923c2d7cd654161a6c84b28a2db65b5f3d. For a protein result, name the benchmark library instead; the DeepProtein README says its legacy graph encoders, Graphormer among them, are not available in its version 2 runtime.

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: Standard transformer blocks over graph nodes with added structural encodings; the benchmark paper names them spatial, centrality and edge encoding. The benchmark's own configuration used one Graphormer layer with eight attention heads.

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: A graph. The package supports the interfaces and datasets of PyG, DGL, OGB and OCP. In the protein benchmark the graph is built from the sequence by way of a SMILES string, with edge features added by an edge featuriser.

strengths.text: The repository ships a container that pins the legacy fairseq, Python and CUDA stack the code needs, with a verification script, so the environment can be rebuilt years after release.

strengths.text: The authors report competition results for the architecture: first place in the quantum prediction track of the OGB Large-Scale Challenge (KDD Cup 2021) and a win in the Open Catalyst Challenge, both claims made by the developers in their README.

run_guide.summary: Build the repository's pinned container and verify that the Graphormer environment imports and preprocesses graphs, on CPU and then on GPU.
prerequisites: Docker, and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit for GPU execution.
Git, to initialise the fairseq submodule.
For the local install instead of the container: a machine matching the pinned CUDA 11.1 wheels.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/microsoft/Graphormer.git
cd Graphormer
git checkout --detach c55f56923c2d7cd654161a6c84b28a2db65b5f3d
steps.explanation: The README gives no clone command, so the clone and the checkout of the commit this page read were added here. The remaining steps are copied from the README.

quotes.text: Initialize the Fairseq submodule and build the image:

steps.title: Initialise the submodule and build the image
steps.shell:
git submodule update --init --recursive
docker build --tag graphormer:legacy .
steps.explanation: Graphormer extends a pinned fairseq revision held as a submodule, so the submodule must be fetched before the image is built.

quotes.text:
git submodule update --init --recursive
docker build --tag graphormer:legacy .

steps.title: Verify the environment on CPU
steps.explanation: Checks that the imports and the graph preprocessing work inside the image.

quotes.text: Verify CPU imports and graph preprocessing:

docker run --rm graphormer:legacy \
    python docker/verify_environment.py

steps.title: Verify the environment on GPU
steps.shell:
docker run --rm --gpus all graphormer:legacy \
    python docker/verify_environment.py --require-cuda
steps.explanation: Repeats the check with CUDA required, which needs the NVIDIA Container Toolkit.

    python docker/verify_environment.py --require-cuda

notes: Two different things carry the name Graphormer here. Microsoft's Graphormer is a fairseq-based training package for graph-level molecule tasks, with pretrained models mentioned but no download address in the README. The protein benchmark result in this database comes from DeepProtein, which trained a single GraphormerLayer from DGL, not Microsoft's package. The paper read was only the arXiv abstract page for 2106.05234, which carries a CC BY-SA 4.0 licence line, so its bytes are not stored. The repository's example training commands and the readthedocs documentation were not fetched.
